'''Cat coat genetics''' determine the colouration, pattern, length, and texture of feline fur. The variations among cat coats are physical properties and should not be confused with cat breeds. A cat may display the coat of a certain breed without actually being that breed. For example, a [[Neva Masquerade]] ([[Siberian cat|Siberian]] colourpoint) could wear [[point colouration]], the coat typically associated with a [[Siamese cat|Siamese]].

== Solid colours ==
{{See also|Introduction to genetics}}

=== Eumelanin and phaeomelanin ===
==== Eumelanin ====
The browning gene ''B/b/b<sup>l</sup>'' codes for ''[[TYRP1]]'' ({{UniProt|Q4VNX8}}), an enzyme involved in the metabolic pathway for eumelanin pigment production. The dominant form, ''B'', will produce black eumelanin. It has two recessive variants, ''b'' (chocolate) and ''b<sup>l</sup>'' (cinnamon), with ''b<sup>l</sup>'' being recessive to both ''B'' and ''b''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lyons |first1=L. A. |last2=Foe |first2=I. T. |last3=Rah |first3=H. C. |last4=Grahn |first4=R. A. |title=Chocolate coated cats: TYRP1 mutations for brown colour in domestic cats |journal=Mammalian Genome |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=356–366 |date=May 2005 |pmid=16104383 |doi=10.1007/s00335-004-2455-4 |s2cid=10054390}}</ref> Chocolate is a rich dark brown colour, and is referred to as chestnut in some breeds. Cinnamon is a light brown which may be a reddish colour.

The [[sex-linked]] red ''"Orange"'' locus, ''O/o'', determines whether a cat will produce phaeomelanin. In cats with orange fur, [[phaeomelanin]] (red pigment) completely replaces [[eumelanin]] (black or brown pigment).<ref name="fanciers">{{cite web |url=http://fanciers.com/other-faqs/color-genetics |title=Cat Colours FAQ: Cat Colour Genetics |work=Fanciers.com |access-date=11 August 2014 |archive-date=28 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140528022342/http://fanciers.com/other-faqs/color-genetics |url-status=dead }}</ref> This gene is located on the [[X chromosome]]. The orange [[allele]] is O, and non-orange is o. Males are typically only orange or non-orange due to only having one X chromosome. Since females have two X chromosomes, they have two alleles of this gene. OO results in orange fur, oo results in fur without any orange (black, brown, etc.), and Oo results in a [[tortoiseshell cat]], in which some parts of the fur are orange and other areas non-orange.<ref name="Peas18">{{Citation |last=Gould |first=Laura| year=2007| edition=2nd |title=Cats Are Not Peas: A Calico History of Genetics| publisher=A. K. Peters, Ltd.| location=Wellesley, Massachusetts |pages=18–19 |isbn=978-1-56881-320-2}}</ref> One in three thousand tortoiseshell cats are male, making the combination possible but rare - however, due to the nature of their genetics, male tortoiseshells often exhibit chromosomal abnormalities.<ref name="Peas175">{{Citation |last=Gould |first=Laura |date=2007 |edition=2nd |title=Cats Are Not Peas: A Calico History of Genetics |publisher=A. K. Peters, Ltd. |location=Wellesley, Massachusetts |page=175 |isbn=978-1-56881-320-2}}</ref> In one study, less than a third of male tortoiseshells had a simple XXY [[Klinefelter syndrome|Klinefelter]]'s karyotype, slightly more than a third were complicated XXY mosaics, and about a third had no XXY component at all (XX/XY or XY/XY mosaics).<ref name="Peas175" />

The coat colour commonly referred to as "orange" is scientifically known as red. Other common names include yellow, ginger, and marmalade. Red show cats have a deep orange colour, but it can also present as a yellow or light ginger colour. Unidentified "rufousing [[polygene]]s" are theorised to be the reason for this variance.
''Orange'' is [[Epistasis|epistatic]] to ''non-agouti'', so all red cats are tabbies. "Solid" red show cats are usually low contrast ticked tabbies.<ref name="Schmidt-Kuntzel-2009">{{cite journal |last1=Schmidt-Küntzel |first1=A. |last2=Nelson |first2=G. |last3=David |first3=V. A. |last4=Schäffer |first4=A. A. |last5=Eizirik |first5=E. |last6=Roelke |first6=M. E. |last7=Kehler |first7=J. S. |last8=Hannah |first8=S. S. |last9=O'Brien |first9=S. J. |last10=Menotti-Raymond |first10=M. |title=A domestic cat X chromosome linkage map and the sex-linked orange locus: mapping of orange, multiple origins and epistasis over nonagouti |journal=Genetics |volume=181 |issue=4 |pages=1415–1425 |date=April 2009 |pmid=19189955 |pmc=2666509 |doi=10.1534/genetics.108.095240}}</ref>

The identity of the gene at the ''Orange'' locus was narrowed down to a 3.5 Mb stretch on the X chromosome in 2009.<ref name="Schmidt-Kuntzel-2009" /> In 2024 it was discovered that the dominant orange colour associated with the ''Orange'' locus is the result of a genomic deletion in a regulatory region of [https://www.wikigenes.org/e/gene/e/158763.html ''ARHGAP36''], a [[Rho family of GTPases|Rho GTPase]] [[GTPase-activating protein|activating protein]]. The ''Dense pigment'' gene, ''D/d'', codes for [[melanophilin]] (''MLPH''; {{UniProt|A0SJ36}}), a protein involved in the transportation and deposition of pigment into a growing hair.<ref name="Schmidt-Kuntzel-2009" /> When a cat has two of the recessive ''d'' alleles (Maltese dilution), black fur becomes "blue" (appearing grey), chocolate fur becomes "lilac" (appearing light, almost greyish brown-lavender), cinnamon fur becomes "fawn", and red fur becomes "cream".<ref name="MBcolour"/> Similar to red cats, all cream cats are tabbies. The ''d'' allele is a single-base deletion that truncates the protein. If the cat has d/d genes, the coat is diluted. If the genes are D/D or D/d, the coat will be unaffected.<ref name="Schmidt-Kuntzel-2009"/>

=== Other genes ===

* ''Barrington Brown'' is a recessive browning gene that dilutes black to mahogany, brown to light brown and chocolate to pale coffee. It is different from the browning gene and has only been observed in laboratory cats.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://messybeast.com/barringtonbrown.htm |title=Recessive Brown - The Enigmatic Barrington Brown Gene |website=messybeast.com |access-date=24 May 2018 |first=Sarah |last=Hartwell}}</ref>
* The ''Dilution modifier'' gene, ''Dm'', "caramelises" the dilute colours as a dominant trait.<ref name="MBcolour">{{Cite web |title=The Basic Self (Solid) Colours of Cats |url= http://messybeast.com/self-solid.htm |access-date=3 July 2025 |website=messybeast.com |first=Sarah |last=Hartwell}}</ref> The existence of this phenomenon as a discrete gene is a controversial subject among feline enthusiasts.{{citation needed|reason=need reference for claim that Dm is controversial|date=July 2025}}
*  ''Amber'', a mutation at the extension locus ''E/e'' (the [[melanocortin 1 receptor]]; ''MC1R'') changes black pigment to amber or light amber, similar in appearance to red and cream. Kittens are born dark but lighten up as they age. Paws and nose still exhibit the original undiluted colour in contrast to other diluted colours, where paws and nose have the diluted colour. This phenomenon was first identified in [[Norwegian Forest Cat]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peterschmitt |first1=M. |last2=Grain |first2=F. |last3=Arnaud |first3=B. |last4=Deléage |first4=G. |last5=Lambert |first5=V. |s2cid=16695179 |title=Mutation in the melanocortin 1 receptor is associated with amber colour in the Norwegian Forest Cat |journal=Animal Genetics |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=547–552 |date=August 2009 |pmid=19422360 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2052.2009.01864.x}}</ref>
* Another recessive mutation at extension was discovered which causes the "russet" colour in [[Burmese cat]]s. It is symbolised as e<sup>r</sup>. Like amber cats, russet cats lighten as they age.<ref name=Gustafon2017>{{cite journal |title=Not Another Type of Potato: MC1R and the Russet Colouration of Burmese Cats  |year=2017 |doi=10.1111/age.12505 |last1=Gustafson |first1=N. A. |last2=Gandolfi |first2=B. |last3=Lyons |first3=L. A. |journal=Animal Genetics |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=116–120 |pmid=27671997}}</ref>
* A modifying factor has also been hypothesised in shaded silver and chinchilla [[Persian cat|Persians]] whose fur turns pale golden in adulthood, due to low levels of phaeomelanin production. These cats resemble shaded or tipped goldens, but are genetically shaded or tipped silvers. This is probably related to the phenomenon known as "tarnishing" in silvers.

==Tabbies==
{{Main|Tabby cat}}

[[File:CAT2007 05 16.jpg|thumb|A mackerel black tabby with the classic "M" on the forehead]]
Tabby cats have a range of variegated and blotched coats, consisting of a dark pattern on a lighter background. This variety is derived from the interplay of multiple genes and resulting phenotypes. Most tabbies feature thin dark markings on the face, including the 'M' on the forehead and an eyeliner effect, pigmented lips and paws, and a pink nose outlined in darker pigment.{{citation needed|date=April 2024}} The following tabby coat patterns are all naturally found in the domestic cat:{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}}
* '''Mackerel''': Thin, dark stripes (sometimes called "tiger stripes").
* '''Blotched/Classic''': Thicker bands or whorls of dark pigment.
* '''Spotted''': Broken bands that look more like individual spots. The flanks only contain spots, no stripes.
* '''Ticked''': No distinct stripes, spots, or blotches on the body—though some may be visible on the legs, face, and tail.

=== Agouti ===
[[File:Poil agouti.svg|thumb|Agouti hair showing alternating bands along the shaft]]
The agouti factor determines the "background" of the tabby coat, which consists of hairs that are banded with dark eumelanin and lighter phaeomelanin along the length of the hair shaft. The ''[[Agouti colouration genetics|Agouti]]'' gene, with its dominant ''A'' allele and recessive ''a'' allele, controls the coding for [[agouti signaling protein|agouti signalling protein]] (''ASIP''; {{UniProt|Q865F0}}). The wild-type dominant ''A'' causes the banding and thus an overall lightening effect on the hair, while the recessive ''non-agouti'' or "hypermelanistic" allele ''a'' does not initiate this shift in the pigmentation pathway. As a result, homozygous ''aa'' have pigment production throughout the entire growth cycle of the hair and therefore along its full length.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eizirik |first1=E. |last2=Yuhki |first2=N. |last3=Johnson |first3=W. E. |last4=Menotti-Raymond |first4=M. |last5=Hannah |first5=S. S. |last6=O'Brien |first6=S. J. |date=March 2003 |title=Molecular genetics and evolution of melanism in the cat family |journal=Current Biology |volume=13 |issue=5 |pages=448–453 |doi=10.1016/S0960-9822(03)00128-3 |pmid=12620197 |s2cid=19021807 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2003CBio...13..448E }}</ref> These homozygotes are solidly dark throughout, which obscures the appearance of the characteristic dark tabby markings—sometimes a suggestion of the underlying pattern, called "[[#Silver and golden series|ghost striping]]", can be seen, especially on kittens and on adults in bright slanted light, in smokes, and sometimes on the forehead, legs, tail or elsewhere.

A major exception to the solid masking of the tabby pattern exists, as the ''O'' allele of the ''O/o'' locus is [[epistatic]] over the ''aa'' genotype. That is, in red or cream coloured cats, tabby marking is displayed regardless of the genotype at the agouti locus. However, some red and most cream tabbies do have a fainter pattern when lacking an agouti allele, indicating that the ''aa'' genotype does still have a faint effect even if it does not induce complete masking. The mechanism of this process is unknown.
[[File:Charcoal Bengal.jpg|thumb|Black charcoal rosetted tabby Bengal kitten with dark "mask"]]

An example of the ''Agouti'' gene can be seen in Bengal cats, which are a hybrid between [[Asian leopard cat]]s and domestic cats. The breed sports the hybrid 'charcoal' pattern, a [[Pseudomelanism|pseudomelanistic]] marking which has a characteristic dark face marking, the "mask", and a broad [[dorsal stripe]] down its back, the "cape".<ref name="Gershony 2014 893–897">{{Cite journal |last1=Gershony |first1=L. C. |last2=Penedo |first2=M. C. T. |last3=Davis |first3=B. W. |last4=Murphy |first4=W. J. |last5=Helps |first5=C. R. |last6=Lyons |first6=L. A. |date=2014-08-20 |title=Who's behind that mask and cape? The Asian leopard cat's ''Agouti'' (''ASIP'') allele likely affects coat colour phenotype in the Bengal cat breed |journal=[[Animal Genetics]] |language=en |volume=45 |issue=6 |pages=893–897 |doi=10.1111/age.12206 |issn=0268-9146 |pmc=4211939 |pmid=25143047 }}</ref> According to Gershoney et al., the charcoal mask is indicated to be the result of a heterozygote of A<sup>Pbe</sup>/a.<ref name="Gershony 2014 893–897"/> The relationships between the different ''agouti'' alleles is not fully understood. More research is required to determine the inheritance modes for charcoal.<ref name="Gershony 2014 893–897"/>

=== Tabby markings ===
The ''Tabby'' locus on chromosome A1 accounts for most tabby patterns seen in domestic cats, including those patterns seen in most breeds. The dominant allele ''Ta<sup>M</sup>'' produces mackerel tabbies, and the recessive ''Ta<sup>b</sup>'' produce classic ('blotched') tabbies.<ref name="Eizirik-2010" /><ref name="OMIALVRN" /> The gene responsible for this differential patterning had been identified as ''transmembrane aminopeptidase Q'' (''Taqpep'', {{UniProt|M3XFH7}}). The gene name ''Taqpep'' has later been replaced by laeverin with symbol ''[[LVRN (gene)|LVRN]]''.<ref name="OMIALVRN">{{Cite web |title=OMIA:001429-9685: Coat colour, tabby in Felis catus (domestic cat) |url=https://omia.org/OMIA001429/9685/ |access-date=2026-03-15 |website=omia.org |publisher=[[Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals]] (OMIA) |via=[[University of Sydney]]}}</ref> A [[threonine]] to [[asparagine]] [[Amino acid replacement|substitution]] at [[amino acid|residue]] 139 ([[Amino acid#Table of standard amino acid abbreviations and properties|T139N]]) in this protein is responsible for producing the tabby phenotype in domestic cats. In [[cheetah]]s, a [[Insertion (genetics)|base pair insertion]] into [[exon|exon 20]] of the protein replaces the 16 C-terminal residues with 109 new ones (N977Kfs110), generating the [[king cheetah]] coat variant.<ref name="taqpep">{{cite journal |last1=Kaelin |first1=C. The wild-type (in [[African wildcat]]s) is the mackerel tabby (stripes look like thin fishbones and may break up into bars or spots). The most common variant is the ''classic'' tabby pattern (broad bands, whorls, and spirals of dark colour on pale background usually with bulls-eye or oyster pattern on flank).<ref name="taqpep" /> Spotted tabbies have their stripes broken up into spots, which may be arranged vertically or horizontally. ==== Ticked tabby ====
The ''Ticked'' (''Ti'') locus on chromosome B1 controls the generation of "ticked coats", agouti coats with virtually no stripes or bars. Ticked tabbies are rare in the random-bred population outside Asia, but fixed in certain breeds such as the [[Abyssinian cat|Abyssinian]] and [[Singapura cat|Singapura]].<ref name="Lyons-2021">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Lyons LA, Buckley RM, Harvey RJ |collaboration=99 Lives Cat Genome Consortium |date=29 March 2021 |title=Mining the 99 Lives Cat Genome Sequencing Consortium database implicates genes and variants for the Ticked locus in domestic cats ( Felis catus ) |journal=Animal Genetics |language=en |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=321–332 |doi=10.1111/age.13059 |issn=0268-9146 |pmc=8252059 |pmid=33780570}}</ref> ''Ti<sup>A</sup>'' is the dominant allele that produces ticked coats; ''Ti<sup>+</sup>'' is the recessive one. The causative gene for ticked tabby markings is ''Dickkopf-related protein 4'' (''[[DKK4]]'').<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kaelin |first1=Christopher B. |last2=McGowan |first2=Kelly A. |last3=Barsh |first3=Gregory S. |date=2021-09-07 |title=Developmental genetics of colour pattern establishment in cats |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=5127 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-25348-2 |pmid=34493721 |issn=2041-1723|pmc=8423757 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12.5127K }}</ref> Both a [[cysteine]] to [[tyrosine]] [[Amino acid replacement|substitution]] at [[Amino acid|residue]] 63 ([[Amino acid#Table of standard amino acid abbreviations and properties|C63Y]]) and an [[alanine]] to [[valine]] substitution at residue 18 ([[Amino acid#Table of standard amino acid abbreviations and properties|A18V]]) result in decreased ''DKK4'', which is associated with ticking. Both variants are present in the Abyssinian breed, and the A18V variant is found in the [[Burmese cat|Burmese]] breed.<ref name="Lyons-2021" /> Stripes often remain to some extent on the face, tail, legs, and sometimes the chest ("bleeding through"). Traditionally, this has been thought to happen in heterozygotes (''Ti<sup>A</sup>Ti<sup>+</sup>'') but be nearly or completely nonexistent in homozygotes (''Ti<sup>A</sup>Ti<sup>A</sup>''). The ticked tabby allele is epistatic to and therefore completely (or mostly) masks all the other tabby alleles, "hiding" the patterns they would otherwise express.<ref name="Eizirik-2010" />

It was once thought that ''Ti<sup>A</sup>'' was an allele of the ''Tabby'' gene, called ''T<sup>a</sup>'', dominant to all other alleles at the locus.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lyons |first1=L. === Other genes ===
[[File:Paintedcats Red Star standing.jpg|thumb|[[Rosette (zoology)|Rosetted]] tabby pattern in a [[Bengal cat|Bengal]].]]

* Other genes (''pattern modifier'' genes) are theorised to be responsible for creating various type of spotting patterns, many of which are variations on a basic mackerel or classic pattern. There are also hypothetical factors which affect the timing and frequency of the agouti shift, affecting agouti band width and the number and quality of alternating bands of eumelanin and phaeomelanin on individual hairs.
* There is a gene not yet identified, but believed to be related to the agouti gene in the [[Chausie]] breed that produces silver-tipped black fur similar to [[Abyssinian cat|Abyssinian]] ticked fur, known as "grizzled". This phenomenon is purported to have been inherited from the [[Felid hybrid|hybridisation]] of the domestic cat to the [[jungle cat]] (''Felis chaus'').
* The rosette tabby pattern is a pattern similar to that of a [[leopard]], where [[Rosette (zoology)|rosette]] spots are spread over the body. The pattern is found in [[Felid hybrid|hybrid]] cat breeds, such as the [[Bengal cat|Bengal]] and [[Safari cat|Safari]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cat Colours and Patterns - Plain English Version |url= http://messybeast.com/colours.htm |access-date=30 March 2023 |website=messybeast.com |first=Sarah |last=Hartwell}}</ref>{{unreliable source?|certain=y|date=October 2023|reason=This is just one random non-expert's blog. It's popular, but it is not a reliable sources for genetic or veterinary information}}
* The ''[[#Silver and golden series|inhibited pigment]]'' gene, ''I/i''. The dominant allele (I) produces ''[[#Tipped|tipped]]'' hairs that are fully coloured only at the tip and have a white base. This allele appears to interact with other genes to produce various degrees of tipping, ranging from deeply tipped silver tabby to lightly tipped shaded silver and chinchilla silver. The inhibitor gene interacts with the non-agouti genotype (I-aa) to produce the colour known as [[#Smoke|smoke]]. The homozygous recessive genotype when combined with the agouti gene (iiA-), produces tabby colouration, which can vary along a spectrum ranging from a deeply patterned brown tabby, to a lighter "golden tabby", to the very lightly coloured shaded or chinchilla golden colours. Red and cream cats with the inhibitor gene (I-O-) are commonly called "[[#Cameo|cameo]]".

== <span class="anchor" id="Tortoiseshells and calicos"></span><span class="anchor" id="Calicos"></span> Tortoiseshells ==
{{Main|Tortoiseshell cat|Calico cat}}

[[File:British Shorthair tricolore.jpg|thumb|Blue tortoiseshell and white (US: diluted calico) [[British Shorthair]]]]

[[Tortoiseshell cat|Tortoiseshell]] is a coat pattern that combines two colours, other than white, in an asymmetrical distribution, either closely mixed ('brindled') or in larger patches.<ref name="Centerwall">{{cite journal |last1=Centerwall|first1=W. R.|last2=Benirschke|first2=K.|date=1973|title=Male Tortoiseshell and Calico (T-C) Cats: Animal models of sex chromosome mosaics, aneuploids, polyploids, and chimerics|journal=Journal of Heredity|volume=64|issue=5|pages=272–278|doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.jhered.a108410|pmid=4798734}}</ref> The two colours always consist of one [[Eumelanin|eumelanistic]] (black, blue, chocolate, lilac, cinnamon or fawn) and one [[Phaeomelanin|phaeomelanistic]] (red or cream) colour. The pattern is caused by [[X-inactivation]], which requires two X chromosomes, consequently the vast majority of tortoiseshells are female, with approximately 1 in 3,000 being male.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.veterinarypartner.com/Content.plx?P=A&A=2209&S=5 |title=The Pet Connection: Feline Fallacies |last=Spadafori |first=Gina |work=VeterinaryPartner.com |access-date=3 July 2008 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080612154655/http://www.veterinarypartner.com/Content.plx?P=A&A=2209&S=5 |archive-date=12 June 2008}}</ref> Male tortoiseshells can occur as a result of chromosomal abnormalities (e.g. [[Klinefelter syndrome]]), by [[mosaic (genetics)|mosaicism]], or by a phenomenon known as [[chimaerism]] (two early stage embryos are merged into a single kitten).

Tortoiseshell should not be mistaken for the natural gradations of colour hues in a tabby pattern. The shades which are present in the ground colour (pale regions) of a tabby are not considered to constitute a separate colour.<ref name="fanciers" /> High degree of warm tones in the ground colour are instead referred to as ''rufousing'' factors or ''rufism''.

=== Tricolour cats ===
Tortoiseshells with [[Piebald|white spotting]] are known as "tricolour" or "tortoiseshell and white".{{Efn|Also known as mi-ke (meaning "triple fur") in Japanese, and lapjeskat (meaning "patches cat") in Dutch.}}<ref name="WCF">{{Cite web |title=Glossary of terms|url=https://wcf.de/en/glossary-of-terms/|access-date=2026-03-03|language=en-US|website=wcf.de|publisher=[[World Cat Federation]]}}</ref> Those with approximately 25–75% white are known in North America as "[[Calico cat|calico]]".<ref name="WCF" /><ref name="Oxford">{{Cite web |title=Calico cat|url=https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/calico-cat|website=oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com|publisher=[[Oxford Learner's Dictionaries]]}}</ref> A tricolour consist of three colours: white, a phaeomelanin red-based colour (red or cream), and eumelanin black-based colour (e.g. black or blue).

[[File:Tortie-white-spotting (no text).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Schematic presentation of how white spotting affects tortoiseshell colour distribution. As the amount of white spotting increases, the tortoiseshell colour becomes less brindled and forms distinct patches of colour. This is related to the migration rates of pigment cells across the surface of the embryo.]]
In tricolour cats, the factor that distinguishes brindled patterns from distinct patches is the placement of eumelanin and phaeomelanin pigment, which is partly dependent on the amount of white, due to an effect of the white spotting gene on the general distribution of melanin. A cat which has both an orange and non-orange gene, Oo, and little to no white spotting, will present with a brindled (mottled) blend of black-based and red-based pigments, reminiscent of [[tortoiseshell]] material (called tortoiseshell cat in the US). An Oo cat with a large amount of white will have bigger, clearly defined patches of black-based and red-based pigments (called a "calico" in the US).

=== Variations ===
* The basic tortoiseshell pattern has several different colours depending on the colour of the eumelanin (the B locus), and dilution (the D locus).
* Tortoiseshell tabbies, also known as ''torbies'', display tabby patterning on both red- and black-based colours. Calico tabbies are colloquially also called ''calibys'' or ''tabicos.''{{Efn|In North American English|name=NAE}}<ref name="fanciers" /> Tortoiseshell cats with small white patches are called ''tortico'' cats, a portmanteau of ''calico'' and ''tortoiseshell''.{{Efn|name=NAE}}<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.merckvetmanual.com/multimedia/table/calico-and-black-and-orange-tortoiseshell-cats | title=Table: Calico and Black and Orange Tortoiseshell Cats }}</ref>{{failed verification|date=November 2024}} Blue tortoiseshell (US: ''diluted calico'') cats have a lighter colouration (blue/cream) and are sometimes called ''calimanco'' or ''clouded tiger''.{{Efn|name=NAE}}<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://www.catster.com/lifestyle/questions-about-calico-cats-answered |title=8 Questions About Calico Cats — Answered |date=14 September 2020}}</ref>

The [[KIT (gene)|''KIT'']] gene determines whether or not there will be any white in the coat, except when a solid white coat is caused by albinism, which happens on a different locus (''C''). White spotting and epistatic white (also known as dominant white) were long thought to be two separate genes (called ''S'' and ''W'' respectively),<ref name="Strain-2015">{{Cite journal |last=Strain |first=George M. |date=2015 |title=The Genetics of Deafness in Domestic Animals |journal=Frontiers in Veterinary Science |language=en |volume=2 |page=29 |doi=10.3389/fvets.2015.00029 |pmid=26664958 |pmc=4672198 |doi-access=free}}</ref> but in fact they are both on the ''KIT'' gene. The two have been combined into a single ''white spotting'' locus (''W''). White spotting can take many forms of particoloured ([[Bicolor cat|bicolour]] or [[Tricolor cat|tricolour]]) patterns, from a small spot of white to the mostly-white Van pattern of the [[Turkish Van]], while epistatic white produces a completely white cat (solid or self white). The ''KIT'' gene ''W'' locus has the following alleles:<ref name="Strain-2015" /><ref name="Górska-2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Górska |first1=Agnieszka |last2=Drobik-Czwarno |first2=Wioleta |last3=Górska |first3=Agata |last4=Bryś |first4=Joanna |date=2 June 2022 |title=Genetic Determination of the Amount of White Spotting: A Case Study in Siberian Cats |journal=Genes |volume=13 |issue=6 |page=1006 |doi=10.3390/genes13061006 |issn=2073-4425 |pmc=9223243 |pmid=35741768 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Dominant White & White Spotting |publisher=Veterinary Genetics Laboratory at the University of California, Davis |url= https://vgl.ucdavis.edu/test/dominant-white-cat |access-date=15 September 2023 |website=VGL.UCDavis.edu}}</ref>
* W<sup>D</sup> (or W)=dominant white (solid/self white), autosomal dominant allele. It causes complete white coat colouration by disrupting replication and migration of [[melanocyte]]s into the skin. The carriers of this allele are white regardless of any other colour-associated gene. It is linked to blue eyes and [[congenital sensorineural deafness in cats|congenital sensorineural deafness]].<ref name="pmid208085813">{{cite journal |last1=Webb |first1=A. A. |last2=Cullen |first2=C. L. |date=June 2010 |title=Coat colour and coat colour pattern-related neurologic and neuro-ophthalmic diseases |journal=Can. Vet. J. |volume=51 |issue=6 |pages=653–657 |pmc=2871368 |pmid=20808581}}</ref> This deafness is due to a reduction in the population and survival of [[melanoblast]] stem cells, which in addition to creating pigment-producing cells, develop into a variety of neurological cell types. White cats with one or two blue eyes have a particularly high likelihood of being deaf. Dominant white is distinct from albinism (''c'') which results from a mutation in a different gene that has no known impact on hearing.
* w<sup>S</sup> (or S)=white spotting (particolour: [[Bicolour cat|bicolour]] or [[Tricolour cat|tricolour]] cats), dominant allele. It only disrupts migration of [[melanocyte]]s to certain patches in the skin, thus leading to the formation of white spots. It exhibits [[codominance]] and variable expression:
** heterozygote (W<sup>h</sup> or ''Ss'')= low degree of spotting white (less than half white); bicolour/tricolour (about half white) or ventral white (about one quarter white — usually the feet, nose, chest, and belly — colloquially known as "tuxedo"), which is dominant to solid colour.
** homozygote (W<sup>l</sup> or ''SS'')= high degree of spotting white (more than half white); dominant harlequin (half to three quarters white) and Van pattern (over three quarters white). The Van pattern is named after the [[Turkish Van]] breed, and expresses as colouration limited to the head and tail.
* w (or N)=wild-type or normal (non-white coats), recessive allele. Homozygotes for it won't have any white in their coat.
* w<sup>g</sup>=[[Birman]] white gloving allele (colloquially known as "mitted"), recessive allele.<ref name="Górska-2022" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montague |first1=M. J. |last2=Li |first2=G. |last3=Gandolfi |first3=B. |last4=Khan |first4=R. |last5=Aken |first5=B. L. |last6=Searle |first6=S. M. |last7=Minx |first7=P. |last8=Hillier |first8=L. In addition to a white tuxedo pattern, hairs are coloured at the root fading into white at the tips, except on the head, where they are often coloured all the way through. It originates in Finland and the name salmiak means "[[salty liquorice]]".<ref name="a600">{{cite journal | last1=Anderson | first1=Heidi | last2=Salonen | first2=Milla | last3=Toivola | first3=Sari | last4=Blades | first4=Matthew | last5=Lyons | first5=Leslie A. | last6=Forman | first6=Oliver P. | last7=Hytönen | first7=Marjo K. | last8=Lohi | first8=Hannes | title=A new Finnish flavour of feline coat colouration, 'salmiak,' is associated with a 95-kb deletion downstream of the KIT gene | journal=Animal Genetics | date=2024-05-09 | volume=55 | issue=4 | pages=676–680 | issn=0268-9146 | doi=10.1111/age.13438 | doi-access=free | pmid=38721753 }}</ref>

== <span class="anchor" id="Colorpoint and albinism"></span><span class="anchor" id="Colourpoint"></span><span class="anchor" id="Colorpoint"></span><span class="anchor" id="Albinism"></span><span class="anchor" id="Albino"></span> Colourpoint and albinism ==
{{See also|Acromelanism}}

The [[Point colouration|colourpoint]] pattern, also known as [[acromelanism]], [[oculocutaneous albinism]] (OCA), and the [[Himalayan cat|Himalayan]] coat-colour pattern,<ref name="OMIATYR">{{Cite web |title=OMIA:000202-9685: Coat/skin colour, oculocutaneous albinism type I (OCA1), TYR-related in Felis catus (domestic cat) |url=https://omia.org/OMIA000202/9685/ |access-date=2026-03-15 |website=omia.org |publisher=[[Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals]] (OMIA) |via=[[University of Sydney]]}}</ref> is most commonly associated with [[Siamese cat|Siamese]] cats, but existed long before the breed's creation and is found worldwide in (non-)pedigree domestic cats. The colloquial point terminology depends on its base colour, e.g. black ("seal", "sable", "brown"), lilac ("frost"), and red ("flame").
 [[File:Flame point shorthair cat.jpg|thumb|"Flame" point domestic short hair cat lounges in a box. This cat also has tabby markings on its forehead.]]

A colourpoint cat has dark colours on their extremities –face, ears, feet, and tail– with a lighter version of the same colour on the rest of the body. This pattern is the result of a [[Mutation#Special classes|temperature sensitive mutation]] causing non-functional form of the [[tyrosinase]] (''TYR'') [[enzyme]] in the [[metabolic pathway]] from [[tyrosine]] to pigment, such as [[melanin]]; thus, a congenital lack of pigment production in the skin, except in the extremities or points where the skin is slightly cooler.<ref name="OMIATYR" /> For this reason, colourpoint cats tend to darken with age as bodily temperature drops; also, the fur may sometimes darken or lighten as a result of temperature change due to illness or significant injury.

More specifically, colourpoint is a type of partial albinism found, together with albinism, on the ''albino'' locus (''C''), which contains the gene ''[[TYR (gene)|TYR]]'' ({{UniProt|P55033}}).<ref name="Schmidt-Kuntzel-2009" /> Although the Siamese colourpoint pattern is the most famous colouration produced by ''TYR'', there are colour mutations at the locus.

* Full colour=''C'' is the wildtype allele resulting in full pigmentation and is completely dominant to all other known alleles at the locus.
* Point=''c<sup>s</sup>'' is the ''point'' allele associated with the Siamese or Himalayan<ref name="OMIATYR" /> colourpoint pattern.
* Sepia=''c<sup>b</sup>'' is an allele called ''sepia'' (or solid), and is most associated with [[Burmese cat]]s. It produces a pattern similar to the Siamese/Himalayan colourpoint, but with a much lower contrast and amber-yellow to green eyes.
* Mink=''c<sup>s</sup>'' and ''c<sup>b</sup>'' are codominant, with ''c<sup>b</sup>/c<sup>s</sup>'' cats having an intermediate phenotype termed ''mink'',<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lyons |first1=L. A. |last2=Imes |first2=D. L. |last3=Rah |first3=H. C. |last4=Grahn |first4=R. A. |date=31 March 2005 |title=Tyrosinase mutations associated with Siamese and Burmese patterns in the domestic cat (Felis catus) |journal=Animal Genetics |language=en |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=119–126 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2052.2005.01253.x |pmid=15771720 |issn=0268-9146|doi-access=free }}</ref> in which the pigment distribution is between sepia and point, and the eye colour is blue-green ([[Aquamarine (color)|aquamarine]]).
* Mocha=''c<sup>m</sup>'' is a novel mutation in Burmese cats that results in a colour pattern named "mocha". Its interactions with other alleles have not yet been fully established.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Y. |last2=Grahn |first2=R. A. |last3=Lyons |first3=L. A. |date=4 February 2019 |title=Mocha tyrosinase variant: a new flavour of cat coat colouration |journal=Animal Genetics |language=en |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=182–186 |doi=10.1111/age.12765 |issn=0268-9146 |pmc=6590430 |pmid=30716167}}</ref>
* Albinism=''c'' and c<sup>2</sup> are two synonymous alleles recessive to all other alleles at the locus that cause [[albinism]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Imes |first1=D. L. |last2=Geary |first2=L. A. |last3=Grahn |first3=R. A. |last4=Lyons |first4=L. A. |date=20 January 2006 |title=Albinism in the domestic cat (Felis catus) is associated with a tyrosinase (TYR) mutation |journal=Animal Genetics |language=en |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=175–178 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2052.2005.01409.x |issn=0268-9146 |pmc=1464423 |pmid=16573534}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abitbol |first1=Marie |last2=Bossé |first2=Philippe |last3=Grimard |first3=Bénédicte |last4=Martignat |first4=Lionel |last5=Tiret |first5=Laurent |date=15 September 2016 |title=Allelic heterogeneity of albinism in the domestic cat |url= https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/age.12503 |journal=Animal Genetics |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=127–128 |doi=10.1111/age.12503|pmid=27634063|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Two distinct alleles causing blue-eyed and pink-eyed albinism respectively have been previously theorised.

The tyrosine pathway also produces [[neurotransmitter]]s, thus mutations in the early parts of that pathway may affect not only pigment, but also neurological development. This results in a higher frequency of [[strabismus|cross-eyes]] among colourpoint cats, as well as the [[White tiger#Genetics and albinism|high frequency of cross-eyes in white tigers]].<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://bigcatrescue.org/white-tigers-are-all-inbred-cross-eyed-and-suffer-greatly/ |title=White Tigers Are All Inbred, Cross Eyed and Suffer Greatly |date=25 November 2008 |website=Big Cat Rescue |access-date=1 January 2020}}</ref>

== <span class="anchor" id="Silver"></span><span class="anchor" id="Golden"></span><span class="anchor" id="Shaded"></span><span class="anchor" id="Tipped"></span><span class="anchor" id="Smoke"></span><span class="anchor" id="Inhibitor"></span><span class="anchor" id="Wide-band"></span><span class="anchor" id="Silver tabby"></span><span class="anchor" id="Cameo"></span> Silver and golden series ==
[[File:Poil agouti.svg|thumb|197x197px|Agouti hair of a brown tabby with phaeomelanin (red pigment) and eumelanin (black or brown pigment).]]

=== Silver series ===
The '''silver''' series is caused by the ''melanin inhibitor'' gene ''I/i''. The dominant form causes melanin production to be suppressed, but it affects phaeomelanin (warm red pigment) much more than eumelanin (black or brown pigment). On tabbies, this turns the background colour into a sparkling cold silver tone. The dark hairs that make the tabby pattern will be silvery-white at their roots, whilst leaving the pigmentation at the tip of these hairs intact, resulting in a cold-toned ''[[silver tabby]]''. On solid cats, it turns the base of the hair throughout their coat into a depigmented pale silvery-white, whilst the tip stays pigmented, making them (''silver'') ''smoke''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=P. |last2=Robinson |first2=R. |title=Melanin inhibitor: a dominant gene in the domestic cat |journal=The Journal of Heredity |volume=71 |issue=6 |pages=427–428 |date=November 1980 |pmid=7217657 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.jhered.a109401}}</ref> The term ''cameo'' is commonly used for red silver and cream silver (inhibitor gene (I-O-)) coloured coats in cats.

=== Wide-band factors ===
Silver agouti cats can have a range of silver tabby phenotypes depending on the depigmentation ratio of the hair root to tip; from regular silver tabby (over half the hair is pigmented), to the more extreme silver tabby forms of silver ''shaded'' (under half the hair is pigmented, approx. {{frac|1|3}} of hair length), and silver ''tipped'' also called 'chinchilla' or 'shell' (only the very tip of the hair is pigmented, approx. {{frac|1|8}} of hair length). This seems to be affected by hypothetical ''wide-band'' factors, which make the silver band at the base of the hair wider in silver tabbies and smokes. Breeders often notate wide-band as a single gene ''Wb/wb'', but it is most likely a [[polygenic]] trait.

=== Golden series ===
If a cat has the wide-band trait but no silver melanin inhibitor, the band will be golden instead of silver. These cats are known as '''golden''' tabbies, or in [[Siberian cat]]s as ''sunshine'' tabbies. The golden colour is caused by the ''[[CORIN]]'' gene. Shaded golden and tipped golden are also possible, in the same hair length distribution as the silver-gene. However, there is no golden smoke, because the combination of wide-band and non-agouti simply produces a solid cat.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://felinegenetics.missouri.edu/feline-research-projects/silver-and-golden |title=Silver and Golden |website=FelineGenetics.Missouri.edu |access-date=1 January 2020 |archive-date=1 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200101043102/http://felinegenetics.missouri.edu/feline-research-projects/silver-and-golden |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url= http://messybeast.com/chinchillas.htm|title=Silver and Gold: Smoke, Shaded and Tipped Cats |website=messybeast.com |access-date=24 May 2018 |first=Sarah |last=Hartwell}}</ref>{{unreliable source?|certain=y|date=October 2023|reason=Random non-expert's blog; it is popular, but it is not a reliable source for genetic or veterinary information.}}

=== Wide-band expression ===
The genetics involved in producing the ideal tabby, tipped, shaded, or smoke cat is complex. Not only are there many interacting genes, but genes sometimes do not express themselves fully, or conflict with one another. For example, the silver melanin inhibitor gene in some instances does not block pigment, resulting in a greyer undercoat, or in [[tarnishing]] (yellowish or rusty fur). The greyer undercoat is considered less desirable to fanciers.

Likewise, poorly-expressed non-agouti or over-expression of melanin inhibitor will cause a pale, washed out black smoke. Various polygenes (sets of related genes), epigenetic factors, or modifier genes, as yet unidentified, are believed to result in different phenotypes of colouration, some deemed more desirable than others by fanciers.

The genetic influences on tipped or shaded cats are:
* [[Agouti coloration genetics|Agouti]] gene.
* Tabby pattern genes (such as T<sup>a</sup> masking the tabby pattern).
* Silver/melanin inhibitor gene ''I/i''.
* Golden ''[[CORIN]]'' gene.
* Factors affecting the number and width of bands of colour on each hair, such as the hypothetical wide-band gene ''wb''. Resulting in shaded or tipped (chinchilla/shell) pigmentation.
* Factors affecting the amount and quality of eumelanin and/or phaeomelanin pigment expression (such as the theorised ''rufousing'' factors)
* Genes causing sparkling appearance (such as ''glitter'' in the [[Bengal cat|Bengal]], ''satin'' in the [[Tennessee Rex]], ''grizzle'' in the [[Chausie]]).
* Factors to clear up residual striping (hypothetical Chaos, Confusion, Unconfused, Erase, and Roan factors).

==Fever coat==
[[File:My adorable little cat (cropped).jpg|thumb|Black and white bicolour kitten with fever coat expression over the black fur]]
'''Fever coat''' is a non-permanent depigmentation effect known in domestic cats, where a female cat experiences health implications during pregnancy (e.g. has a [[fever]] or is stressed), causing her unborn kittens' fur to develop a frosty silver-type colour (silver-grey, cream, or reddish) rather than what the kitten's [[genetics]] would normally show. The depigmentation is most prominent at the hair tips, rather than the roots as would be the case in actual silver coats. After birth, the frost-like fur is replaced naturally by fur in their actual genetic colours during a [[Moulting|moult]] in their first year; in most cases the full colour is completely grown in at 6–8 months old.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=The indefinable kitten colours |url=http://messybeast.com/indefinable-colours-kittens.htm |access-date=2026-03-13 |website=messybeast.com |first=Sarah |last=Hartwell}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=7 Kittens Born with 'Fever Coat', Their True Colours Begin to Show As They Grow |url= http://www.lovemeow.com/7-kittens-born-with-fever-coat-their-true-colors-begin-to-show-as-they-grow-2532020501.html |work=LoveMeow.com |date=7 February 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.meowingtons.com/blogs/lolcats/amazing-color-changing-kittens |title=Amazing Colour-changing Kittens: What Is Fever Coat? |publisher=Meowingtons |date=20 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Unique Litter of Kittens Born With 'Fever Coat'. But What Is 'Fever Coat'? |url=http://thebestcatpage.com/2017/02/22/unique-litter-kittens-born-fever-coat-fever-coat/ |work=TheBestCatPage.com |date=22 February 2017 |access-date=24 May 2018 |archive-date=25 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180525062418/http://thebestcatpage.com/2017/02/22/unique-litter-kittens-born-fever-coat-fever-coat/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Fur length and texture ==

=== Cat coat hair ===
[[File:Down Awn and guard hairs of cat 2012 11 13 9203r.JPG|thumb|upright=1|Down, awn and guard hairs of a domestic tabby cat]]
Cat fur can be short, long, curly, or hairless. Most cats are short-haired, like their [[African wildcat|wild ancestor]].<ref name="Bryan-2021">{{Cite book |last=Bryan |first=Kim |url= https://www.worldcat.org/title/1255796262 |title=The complete cat breed book - choose the perfect cat for you |publisher=[[Dorling Kindersley Limited]] |year=2021 |isbn=978-0-241-44631-7 |edition=2nd |location=London}}</ref> The fur can naturally come in three types of hairs; [[Guard hair|guard]], [[Awn hair|awn]], and [[down hair]]. The length, density and proportions of these three hairs varies greatly between breeds, and in some cats only one or two types are found.<ref name="Bryan-2021" /><ref name="spruce">{{Cite web |title=What Is the Difference Between Cat Hair and Fur? |url=https://www.thesprucepets.com/cat-fur-vs-hair-554813 |access-date=2023-10-13 |website=The Spruce Pets |language=en}}</ref>

Most oriental breeds only express one single layer of silky coat.<ref name="Bryan-2021" /> However, cats can also have double-layered coats out of two hair types in which the down hairs form the soft, insulating undercoat, and the guard hairs form the protective outer coat.<ref name="Bryan-2021" />

A typical cat coat exists of all three natural hair types, but due to the equal lengths of two of these hairs, the coat is still considered double-layered.<ref name="Bryan-2021" /> Typically, the down hairs comprise the undercoat while the guard and awn hairs make up the basic top coat.<ref name="Bryan-2021" /><ref name="spruce" /> Double-coated cats with thick undercoats require daily grooming as these coats are more prone to matting.<ref name="Bryan-2021" /> Double coats are found in for example the [[Persian cat|Persian]], [[British Shorthair]], [[Maine Coon]] and [[Norwegian Forest Cat]].

Additionally, there even exist cats which express all three natural types of cat hair in different lengths and structures, which form three different layers. These cats are called triple-coated. [[Siberian cat|Siberians]] and [[Neva Masquerade]]s are known for their unique triple coats,<ref name="Bryan-2021" /> which provided their [[landrace]] ancestors with extra insulation to withstand their arctic habitat.

=== Coat mutations ===
There have been many genes identified that result in unusual cat fur. These genes have been discovered in random-bred and purebred cats worldwide, and are sometimes [[selectively bred]] into new breeds or breed varieties. Some of the genes are in danger of going extinct because the cats are not sold beyond the region where the mutation originated or there is simply not enough demand for cats expressing the mutation.

In many breeds, coat gene mutations are perceived as unfavourable. An example is the [[Rex cat|rex]] allele which appeared in Maine Coons in the early 1990s in Germany, the UK and the US.

==== Fur length ====
Cat fur length is governed by the ''Length'' gene in which the dominant form, ''L'', codes for short hair, and the recessive ''l'' codes for long hair. In the longhaired cat, the transition from [[anagen]] (hair growth) to [[catagen]] (cessation of hair growth) is delayed due to this mutation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Drögemüller |first1=C. |last2=Rüfenacht |first2=S. |last3=Wichert |first3=B. |last4=Leeb |first4=T. |date=June 2007 |title=Mutations within the FGF5 gene are associated with hair length in cats |journal=Animal Genetics |volume=38 |issue=3 |pages=218–221 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2052.2007.01590.x |pmid=17433015}}</ref> A rare recessive shorthair gene has been observed in some lines of (silver) Persian where two longhaired parents have produced shorthaired offspring.

The ''Length'' gene has been identified as the [[fibroblast growth factor 5]] (''FGF5''; {{UniProt|M3X9S6}}) gene. The dominant allele codes for the short coat is seen in most cats. Long coats are coded for by at least four different recessively inherited mutations, the alleles of which have been identified.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kehler |first1=J. S. |last2=David |first2=V. A. |last3=Schäffer |first3=A. A. |last4=Bajema |first4=K. |last5=Eizirik |first5=E. |last6=Ryugo |first6=D. K. |last7=Hannah |first7=S. S. |last8=O'Brien |first8=S. J. |last9=Menotti-Raymond |first9=M. |date=September 2007 |title=Four independent mutations in the feline fibroblast growth factor 5 gene determine the long-haired phenotype in domestic cats |journal=The Journal of Heredity |volume=98 |issue=6 |pages=555–566 |doi=10.1093/jhered/esm072 |pmc=3756544 |pmid=17767004}}</ref> The most ubiquitous is found in most or all long haired breeds while the remaining three are found only in Ragdolls, Norwegian Forest Cats, and Maine Coons.
[[File:Wavy fur of a Devon Rex cat.jpg|thumb|Wavy fur of a Devon Rex cat]]

==== Curly-coated ====
{{main|Rex mutation}}

There are various genes producing curly-coated or "rex" cats. New types of rex arise spontaneously in random-bred cats now and then. Some of the rex genes that breeders have selected for are:

* [[Devon Rex]]
** Mutation in ''[[KRT71]]'' ({{UniProt|E1AB55}}), the same gene causing hairlessness in [[Sphynx cat|Sphynx]] cats. ''re'' is an allele completely recessive to the wildtype and completely dominant to ''hr'' found in Sphynx.<ref name="pmid20953787">{{cite journal |last1=Gandolfi |first1=B |last2=Outerbridge |first2=CA |last3=Beresford |first3=LG |last4=Myers |first4=JA |last5=Pimentel |first5=M |last6=Alhaddad |first6=H |last7=Grahn |first7=JC |last8=Grahn |first8=RA |last9=Lyons |first9=LA |title=The naked truth: Sphynx and Devon Rex cat breed mutations in KRT71. |journal=Mammalian Genome |date=October 2010 |volume=21 |issue=9–10 |pages=509–515 |doi=10.1007/s00335-010-9290-6 |pmid=20953787|pmc=2974189}}</ref>
* [[Cornish Rex]]
** Mutation in ''[[LPAR6]]'' ({{UniProt|A0A5F5XLZ8}}). A completely recessive allele termed ''r''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gandolfi |first1=Barbara |last2=Alhaddad |first2=Hasan |last3=Affolter |first3=Verena K. |last4=Brockman |first4=Jeffrey |last5=Haggstrom |first5=Jens |last6=Joslin |first6=Shannon E. * [[Ural Rex]]
** Mutation in ''[[LIPH (gene)|LIPH]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Manakhov |first1=A. D. |last2=Andreeva |first2=T. V. |last3=Rogaev |first3=E. * [[German Rex]]
** Provisionally an allele termed ''gr''. Same [[Locus (genetics)|locus]] as Cornish, but proposed as a different [[allele]]. However, most breeders consider the German Rex to have ''r''/''r'' genotype.
* [[Oregon Rex]] (extinct)
** A hypothetical recessive allele termed ''ro''.
* [[Selkirk Rex]]
** A [[Dominance (genetics)#Dominant allele|dominant]] allele termed ''Se'', although sometimes described as an [[Dominance (genetics)#Incomplete dominance|incomplete dominant]] because the three possible allele pairings relate to three different phenotypes: heterozygous cats (''Se/se'') may have a fuller coat that is preferred in the show ring, while homozygous cats (''Se/Se'') may have a tighter curl and less coat volume. (''se/se'' type cats have a normal coat.) This phenomenon may also colloquially be referred to as additive dominance.
* [[LaPerm]]
** Provisional completely dominant ''Lp'' allele.

==== Hairlessness ====
There are also genes for hairlessness:
* h=French hairless cat, [[Recessive gene#Recessive allele|recessive]].
* hd=British hairless cat, [[Recessive gene#Recessive allele|recessive]].
* Hp=[[Donskoy cat|Russian Donskoy]] and [[Peterbald]], [[Dominance (genetics)#Dominant allele|dominant]].
* hr=[[Sphynx cat]], [[Recessive gene#Recessive allele|recessive]]. Identified on ''[[KRT71]]''.<ref name="pmid20953787"/>

Some rex cats are prone to temporary hairlessness, known as baldness, during [[moulting]].

Here are a few other genes resulting in unusual fur:
* The ''Wh'' gene (dominant, possibly incomplete) results in [[American Wirehair|Wirehair]] cats. They have bent or crooked hair producing springy, crinkled fur.
* A hypothetical ''Yuc'' gene, or [[York Chocolate]] undercoat gene, results in cats with no undercoat. However, the proportional relationship between [[Guard hair|guard]], [[Awn hair|awn]], and [[down hair]] production varies greatly between all breeds.
* A recessive autosomal gene for ''Onion hair'' which causes roughness and swelling on the hairs. The swelling is due to enlargement of the inner core of medulla cells.
* A recessive autosomal gene ''spf'' for ''sparse fur''. As well as sparse coat, the hairs are thin, straggly and contorted and there is brown exudate around the eyes and nose and on the chest and stomach. A similar condition is linked to [[Ornithine Transcarbamylase Deficiency]] in mice.
